heading: Background
html:
Osteoarthritis of the hip and knee is a clinical diagnosis in patients ≥45 with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness lasting ≤30 minutes (NICE NG226). Joint replacement is highly effective for end-stage disease, but outcomes are best when patients arrive optimised and with realistic expectations.

Referral is for consideration of arthroplasty. The decision is made jointly with the surgeon — but the referral should only be made if the patient is willing in principle to consider an operation. Patients not willing to consider surgery are better served by MSK services.

heading: Assessment
html:
• Pain: severity, night/rest pain, analgesia use and effect.
  • Function: walking distance, stairs, sleep disturbance, work/caring roles, use of aids.
  • Examination: gait, range of movement, fixed deformity, effusion; check the hip in 'knee pain' (referred pain is common).
  • Imaging: weight-bearing AP knee (plus skyline/lateral) or AP pelvis for hip. A recent X-ray is required for triage, but radiographic severity alone does not determine referral — correlate with symptoms.
  • Whole patient: BMI, comorbidities, frailty and functional baseline, patient expectations and willingness for surgery.

Atypical features? Rest pain out of proportion, rapid deterioration over weeks, or risk factors (steroids, alcohol, previous fracture) — consider avascular necrosis or rapidly progressive OA and refer urgently.

heading: Primary care management
html:
All patients should have tried core treatment (NICE NG226) before referral:

  • Therapeutic exercise — structured strengthening; MSK physiotherapy via the Single Access Point (030 3333 3001) or NHS Inform resources.
  • Weight management — any sustained loss helps symptoms and surgical risk; refer to weight management services where appropriate.
  • Analgesia: topical NSAID first-line for knee (e.g. topical Ibuprofen); oral NSAID (e.g. Naproxen) with gastroprotection (Omeprazole) at the lowest effective dose. Avoid long-term opioids — they do not improve outcomes and complicate perioperative care.
  • Walking aids and activity pacing.
  • Intra-articular corticosteroid injection for short-term relief of a painful flare, where available.

heading: Who to refer
html:
Urgent orthopaedic referral / same-day discussion

  • Suspected avascular necrosis
  • Rapidly progressive joint destruction
  • New symptoms in a joint with previous surgery / prosthesis (discuss — do not aspirate a prosthetic joint in the community)
  • Suspected septic arthritis — see the hot swollen joint pathway

Routine referral for consideration of arthroplasty — all of:

  • Clinically and radiologically confirmed OA
  • Substantial impact on quality of life (pain including night/rest pain, functional limitation) despite core non-surgical treatment
  • Patient willing to consider surgery

Include in the referral (supports triage and avoids delay): X-ray report and date; analgesia tried; physiotherapy/weight management undertaken; BMI; comorbidities; frailty and baseline function; explicit confirmation the patient would consider surgery.

Do not delay referral solely because of BMI, age or smoking status (NICE NG226) — but do flag optimisation opportunities so the service can act on them in parallel.

heading: Who not to refer
html:
• Patients not willing to consider surgery — continue core treatment and MSK support; re-refer if their position changes.
  • Patients who have not yet tried core treatment (exercise, weight management, adequate analgesia) — refer to MSK services first.
  • Asymptomatic or mild radiographic OA — X-ray changes alone are not an indication.
  • Acute flare in otherwise manageable OA — treat the flare (analgesia ± injection) and reassess.
